title: GPU Memory Hierarchy
summary: Global, shared, and per-thread memory on a GPU, and the coalescing rule that decides whether you actually get the bandwidth on the spec sheet.

slides.markdown:
**Global memory** is the GPU's main pool — several gigabytes of dedicated DRAM (GDDR or HBM), accessible to every thread on the chip. It's where input data starts and where final results land.

It's also, relative to on-chip storage, **high latency**: hundreds of cycles to service a request. A GPU tolerates this not by making global memory faster, but by keeping so many warps in flight that while one waits on a global-memory request, others have real work to do — the same latency-hiding-via-occupancy trick that shapes the whole architecture ([gpu-architecture-fundamentals](gpu-architecture-fundamentals)).

**Shared memory** is a small, fast, on-chip scratchpad — tens of kilobytes per **thread block** — that the programmer explicitly manages. Unlike a CPU cache, it isn't automatically populated; the kernel writes data into it deliberately, then every thread in that block can read it at near-register speed.

The payoff: if multiple threads in a block need the same piece of global data, loading it into shared memory once and letting all threads reuse it from there avoids dozens of redundant, high-latency global-memory round-trips. This is the single biggest lever GPU kernel authors have for performance.

Each thread gets its own **registers** — the fastest storage on the chip, private and not shared with any other thread. Registers hold a thread's working variables (loop counters, intermediate sums) for the duration of the kernel.

When a kernel needs more per-thread storage than the register file can supply, the compiler spills the overflow to **local memory** — which, despite the name, physically lives in the same slow global DRAM. Heavy register spilling silently turns what looks like fast per-thread state into expensive global-memory traffic.

The memory hierarchy mirrors the thread/block/grid execution hierarchy exactly: registers are per-thread, shared memory is per-block, global memory is grid-wide.

![The GPU memory hierarchy — registers per thread, shared memory per block, global memory shared across the whole grid](assets/gpu-memory-hierarchy.svg)

That symmetry isn't a coincidence: memory scope was designed to match the natural boundaries of parallel work, so threads that cooperate (same block) get a fast shared channel, while threads that don't (different blocks) only meet in the slow, common global pool.

assets.alt: The GPU memory hierarchy — registers per thread, shared memory per block, global memory shared across the whole grid

slides.markdown:
**Memory coalescing** is the rule that decides whether a warp's memory requests turn into one wide transaction or many small ones. If adjacent threads in a warp access adjacent addresses (thread 0 reads element 0, thread 1 reads element 1, ...), the memory controller **merges** them into a single wide burst.

This single rule is why GPU bandwidth numbers on a spec sheet are only achievable with the right access pattern — the hardware isn't rewarding cleverness, it's just able to serve one request instead of thirty-two when the addresses line up.

A **strided or scattered** access pattern — thread `i` reading element `i * stride` for some stride greater than 1, or threads reading effectively random addresses — defeats coalescing entirely. What could have been one 128-byte transaction becomes up to 32 separate ones.

This is the single most common reason a GPU kernel underperforms its theoretical bandwidth: the compute logic can be correct and even well-parallelized, yet a column-major access on a row-major array (or vice versa) alone can cost an order of magnitude in throughput. Structuring data layout for coalesced access is often the highest-leverage optimization available.

slides.subTitle: The scratchpad has its own hidden coalescing rule
slides.markdown:
Shared memory is physically split into multiple **banks** (commonly 32, matching warp size) so that many threads can access it simultaneously — one access per bank per cycle. If every thread in a warp reads a **different bank**, all accesses complete in one cycle.

A **bank conflict** happens when multiple threads in the same warp hit the *same* bank in the same cycle — those accesses serialize instead of running in parallel, directly costing cycles. A common trigger: an array of stride 32 accessed by consecutive threads (`data[threadIdx.x * 32]`) — every thread lands on the exact same bank, turning what should be one fast cycle into 32 serialized ones. This is the shared-memory equivalent of global memory's coalescing rule, and kernel authors routinely pad array dimensions (adding one unused element per row) specifically to break this exact stride pattern.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: the real cost of uncoalesced access
slides.subTitle: One 128-byte transaction versus thirty-two 32-byte ones
slides.markdown:
A warp of 32 threads each reads one 4-byte float, fully coalesced (adjacent addresses) versus fully scattered (random addresses):

```
coalesced:   32 threads * 4 bytes = 128 bytes -> 1 memory transaction
scattered:   32 threads * 4 bytes, each its own transaction
             -> up to 32 transactions, each fetching a minimum granule
             (e.g. 32 bytes even though only 4 are used)

effective bytes moved (scattered) = 32 * 32 = 1024 bytes for 128 bytes of useful data
bandwidth efficiency = 128 / 1024 = 12.5%
```

The scattered access pattern doesn't just take more transactions — it moves roughly 8x more bytes off DRAM than the kernel actually needed, because each small transaction still costs a minimum fetch granule. This is precisely why a kernel that seems compute-light can still run far below peak: the achieved memory bandwidth, not the theoretical peak, is what the arithmetic-intensity math in [Roofline Model](roofline-model) actually uses.

slides.subTitle: Two different bets on how to get bandwidth
slides.markdown:
| | GDDR (e.g. GDDR6) | HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) |
|---|---|---|
| Physical layout | Separate chips on the board, wide traces | Stacked DRAM dies directly on/near the GPU package |
| Bus width | Wide but bounded by board routing | Extremely wide (thousands of bits) via stacking |
| Bandwidth | High | Higher, at lower power per bit moved |
| Cost | Lower | Higher (advanced packaging) |
| Typical use | Consumer/gaming GPUs | Datacenter accelerators, HPC, top-tier ML training GPUs |

Both solve the same problem — global memory bandwidth is usually the real limiter on GPU throughput, not compute — but HBM buys more bandwidth per watt by physically stacking memory dies close to the compute die, at a manufacturing cost premium only datacenter-tier products typically justify.
